opus-5.5.text:
I think the potential is enormous, honestly larger than most of the markets we've seen digital AI transform so far. If you look at the global economy, the vast majority of it is physical. It's manufacturing, logistics, transportation, agriculture, construction, healthcare. People moving things, building things, caring for people. Digital AI, language models and so on, mostly touch the part of the economy that happens on screens and in documents. That's very valuable, but it's a fraction of the whole.

Physical AI is about giving machines the ability to perceive, understand, and act in the real world. Once you can do that reliably, every machine that moves becomes a candidate: cars, trucks, warehouse robots, factory arms, humanoids, drones, even the buildings and factories themselves as large autonomous systems. So when people ask about market size, I like to think of it less as a single market and more as a layer that sits on top of a huge portion of the global GDP, tens of trillions of dollars of activity.

There's also a labor angle. Many countries are facing aging populations and labor shortages, especially in manufacturing and elder care. Physical AI isn't only about efficiency there. It's about whether we can sustain the things society needs at all.

That said, I want to be realistic about the timeline. Physical AI is harder than digital AI in some fundamental ways. Data is scarce. You can't just scrape the internet for robot interaction data the way we did for text. Mistakes are costly, because a robot that hallucinates can break things or hurt someone. And the hardware has to be good, cheap, and robust. That's why I believe so much in simulation, world models, and synthetic data. They let us generate the experience these systems need to learn safely and at scale before deploying them.

So my view is: the ceiling is enormous, possibly the largest opportunity in the history of computing, but it will unfold in stages. Autonomous driving and industrial robotics first, then more general-purpose robots as the foundation models and the data infrastructure mature. We're still early, which is exactly what makes it exciting.

r001.rationale: It cites aging populations in many countries as a pressure that Physical AI could address, supporting market growth.

fable-5.1.text:
I think Physical AI is going to be the largest market that AI touches, and I don't say that lightly. If you look at what we've done so far with generative AI and language models, we've mostly been automating knowledge work, things that happen inside a computer. That's a big market, but the physical world is much bigger. Transportation, manufacturing, logistics, agriculture, healthcare, construction, every one of these industries involves machines interacting with the physical world, and today almost all of that still requires a human in the loop.

If you just add up the robotics and automation industries as they exist today, you're already talking about hundreds of billions of dollars. But that's the wrong way to think about it, because today's robots are very limited. They work in highly structured environments, doing repetitive tasks, and they're programmed by experts. What Physical AI changes is that machines can perceive, reason, and act in unstructured environments. That means every car can become a robot, every factory can be more flexible, and we can start to have humanoid robots doing work in places where it was never economical to automate before.

So I think the right way to size it is to look at the labor market itself. Globally, there are billions of people doing physical work, and the economic value of that work is in the tens of trillions of dollars. Even if Physical AI augments only a small fraction of it, you're talking about a multi-trillion-dollar opportunity. And honestly, I think the demand is there because of demographics. Many countries are facing labor shortages and aging populations. There simply aren't enough people to do the work that needs to be done.

That said, I want to be realistic about the timeline. Physical AI is harder than language. The physical world is governed by laws of physics, data is expensive to collect, and mistakes have real consequences. So the market will develop in waves. Autonomous vehicles and industrial robots will come first, then more general-purpose robots in warehouses and factories, and eventually humanoids in homes. It will take years, maybe a decade or more, to fully realize. But the direction is clear, and the size of the prize is why so many of us are working on it.

r001.rationale: The response cites aging populations, alongside labor shortages, as a reason demand for Physical AI will be high.

astra-6.text:
I think the potential is enormous, because Physical AI extends AI from processing information to doing useful work in the physical world. That could include manufacturing, logistics, transportation, and eventually tasks in our homes.

But I would distinguish the potential market from how quickly we can reach it. A robot has to be reliable, safe, and economically useful in a real environment. Being able to demonstrate a task is very different from doing it consistently every day at a competitive cost.

So I wouldn’t put a precise number on it. I’d expect adoption to start with specific tasks where the value is clear and the environment is relatively controlled, then expand as the technology improves. The long-term opportunity is much broader than selling robots—it includes the value of the work those systems can perform.

r001.rationale: The response describes broad applications and potential market growth, but does not identify population aging as a reason for a large Physical AI market.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the potential is enormous, because Physical AI brings intelligence into the physical world—into robots, vehicles, factories, and the machines we use every day. The opportunity goes beyond selling robots. It includes the software, computing, simulation, and services that make those systems useful.

I would be cautious about putting a precise number on it. The addressable market could be measured in trillions of dollars, but that is different from saying how quickly revenue will materialize. Adoption will depend on reliability, safety, cost, and whether a system delivers a clear return on investment.

My expectation is that progress will happen task by task. We’ll first see deployment where the environment is relatively controlled and the economic value is easy to measure. As the technology becomes more capable and affordable, the range of applications will expand.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the market opportunity to physical-world applications and related software, computing, simulation, and services, but does not identify population aging as a reason for a large market.
